sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch, downtown Boston (1.5 km radius, 200 geotagged articles)

stops.name: Boston Common
stops.description: The oldest city park in the country, set aside in 1634 as a cow pasture and militia field, and the starting point of the Freedom Trail.

stops.name: Massachusetts State House
stops.description: The 1798 Bulfinch capitol on Beacon Hill, whose dome Paul Revere's company first sheathed in copper before it was gilded in gold leaf.

stops.name: Robert Gould Shaw Memorial
stops.description: Augustus Saint-Gaudens' bronze relief of the all-Black 54th Massachusetts marching out of the city in 1863, the first American civic monument to honor Black soldiers.

stops.name: Boston Athenaeum
stops.description: A membership library founded in 1807 that still holds most of the books George Washington kept at Mount Vernon.

stops.name: Park Street Church
stops.description: Its 217-foot steeple made it the tallest building in the United States from 1810 to 1828, and the gunpowder stored here during the War of 1812 helped earn the corner its Brimstone nickname.

stops.name: Granary Burying Ground
stops.description: Boston's third-oldest cemetery, opened in 1660, where Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock and the five victims of the Boston Massacre are buried.

stops.name: King's Chapel
stops.description: Peter Harrison's 1754 granite chapel, whose wooden predecessor was taken apart and shipped to Nova Scotia to become another church.

stops.name: Old City Hall
stops.description: Boston's French Second Empire city hall from 1865 to 1969, now offices, with a statue of Benjamin Franklin in the courtyard marking the site of the first public school in America.

stops.name: Omni Parker House
stops.description: The longest continuously operating hotel in the United States, open since 1855 and still trading on the pastry and the dinner roll that carry its name.

stops.name: Boston Irish Famine Memorial
stops.description: Two 1998 bronze groups on a small downtown plaza, one family starving in Ireland and one arriving in Boston, marking the migration that reshaped the city.

stops.name: Old Corner Bookstore
stops.description: Built in 1718 and now Boston's oldest commercial building, it was the publishing house where Emerson, Hawthorne and Longfellow gathered at Parnassus Corner.

stops.name: Old South Meeting House
stops.description: Thousands packed this 1729 meeting hall on the night of December 16, 1773 before walking out to dump the tea in the harbor.

stops.name: Old State House
stops.description: Boston's oldest surviving public building, from whose balcony the Declaration of Independence was first read to the city in July 1776.

stops.name: Boston Massacre Site
stops.description: A cobblestone ring in the traffic island outside the Old State House marks where British soldiers fired on a crowd on March 5, 1770.

stops.name: Faneuil Hall
stops.description: The market and meeting hall nicknamed the Cradle of Liberty, still topped by Shem Drowne's 1742 grasshopper weathervane.

note: Boston, MA - never run before, and alphabetically first among the untouched NFL cities (only Atlanta and Baltimore appear in nightly.json history). All 15 stops sit inside the Freedom Trail's downtown core, a walkable loop of roughly a mile from Boston Common up to Faneuil Hall. Every stop was opened individually on Wikipedia and confirmed still standing and publicly visible; the Shaw Memorial was removed for conservation in 2020 and has since been reinstalled in its original spot. Two addresses have a street but no house number, and neither was invented from coordinates: the Shaw Memorial (opposite 24 Beacon St, ZIP taken from 10 1/2 Beacon St a few doors along) and the Boston Massacre Site (a marker in the State St traffic island, ZIP from the adjacent Old State House). Boston Common's 139 Tremont St is the visitor-center address for a 50-acre park, so a human may want to re-pin it. Also verified but held back to keep the batch at 15: the Winthrop Building (7 Water St, 02109, Boston's first steel-frame skyscraper) and the Brewer Fountain (on the Common at Tremont and Park, no street number). Dropped from the sweep: King's Chapel Burying Ground (same address as King's Chapel), and the many GeoSearch hits that turned out to be demolished buildings, vanished streets or squares rather than places to stand - Scollay Square, Province House, Hancock Manor, the Tremont House hotel and similar. Freedom Trail sites north of Faneuil Hall (Paul Revere House, Old North Church, USS Constitution, Bunker Hill Monument) were left out deliberately as outliers from this walkable cluster; they are worth their own Boston batch later.
